summary: Specifies how GMPLS extensions are encoded in the OSPF routing protocol. It is a standards-track document that complements the general GMPLS routing document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4203 defines extra link details that OSPF routers can share for GMPLS. These details describe how a link is identified, protected, switched, and provisioned with bandwidth.

subtitle: How OSPF advertises the link details that GMPLS needs for optical and other non-packet networks.

tldr.problem: GMPLS needs routing advertisements to describe link identifiers, protection, shared risks, switching capabilities, and bandwidth. The existing OSPF traffic-engineering link format did not define all of these details.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4203 adds four sub-TLVs to the OSPF Traffic Engineering Link TLV and defines a link-local opaque LSA for exchanging a link identifier with a neighbor.
tldr.outcome: It specifies the encodings for these GMPLS link details and updates RFC 3630. RFC 4203 has since been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002, and RFC 7074.

today: RFC 4203 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3630. It has since been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002, and RFC 7074.

sections.title: GMPLS Details in OSPF Traffic Engineering Advertisements
sections.content:
OSPF routers can advertise traffic-engineering properties in opaque link-state advertisements (LSAs). An LSA is a routing message that describes network state. RFC 4203 defines how these advertisements carry the link information needed by Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS).

The existing Traffic Engineering LSA contains a Link TLV, a typed field that can hold nested sub-TLVs. This RFC adds four Link sub-TLVs: link local and remote identifiers, link protection type, interface switching capability, and shared risk link groups.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 4203 adds four kinds of link information to OSPF traffic-engineering messages. Routers can use these fields to describe the links that GMPLS can select.

sections.title: Identifiers for Unnumbered Links
sections.content:
Sub-TLV type 11 carries a Link Local Identifier followed by a Link Remote Identifier. Each identifier is four octets, so the value is eight octets long. These identifiers name an unnumbered link, which has no IP address assigned to the link.

If a router does not yet know the remote identifier, it sets that value to zero. A router can send its own local identifier to its neighbor using the link-local LSA described later in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router assigns an identifier to its end of an unnumbered link. The sub-TLV carries both identifiers, and the remote value is zero when it is not known.

sections.title: Protection Types and Shared Risks
sections.content:
Sub-TLV type 14 describes link protection. Its four-octet value begins with a bit vector: the defined capabilities include Extra Traffic, Unprotected, Shared, Dedicated 1:1, Dedicated 1+1, and Enhanced. The remaining three octets are reserved; senders SHOULD set them to zero and receivers SHOULD ignore them. This sub-TLV may appear at most once in a Link TLV.

Sub-TLV type 16 carries an unordered list of 32-bit Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) values. An SRLG identifies links that share a risk, and this sub-TLV may also appear at most once in the Link TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: One field lists the protection methods available for a link. Another lists shared-risk group numbers, so a path planner can identify links that belong to the same risk group.

sections.title: Interface Switching Capability and Bandwidth
sections.content:
Sub-TLV type 15 describes an interface's switching capability and encoding, followed by eight maximum LSP bandwidth values, one for each priority from 0 through 7. Each bandwidth value uses four octets in IEEE floating-point format, measured in bytes per second. The remaining fields depend on the switching capability.

For PSC-1 through PSC-4, the value also includes minimum LSP bandwidth, a two-octet interface MTU, and padding. For TDM it includes minimum bandwidth, an indication for Standard or Arbitrary SONET/SDH, and padding. L2SC and LSC have no additional capability-specific information. The sub-TLV may appear more than once when an interface has multiple switching capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: This field describes the kind of traffic an interface can switch and its available bandwidth at each priority. Some switching types also carry a minimum bandwidth, an interface size, or a SONET/SDH indication.

sections.title: Restart Behavior and Neighbor Identifier Exchange
sections.content:
During restart, a router advertises zero unreserved bandwidth and a Traffic Engineering metric of 0xffffffff until it can determine which resources remain available. For links with LSC or FSC switching capability, it also advertises zero maximum LSP bandwidth during this period. Before a planned restart, the router SHOULD advertise zero bandwidth to discourage new LSP setup through it.

For information needed only by the neighbor on a particular interface, the RFC defines a TE Link Local LSA. It has link-local flooding scope and carries a Link Local Identifier TLV with a 32-bit identifier. On an unnumbered point-to-point link, one router's local identifier is the neighbor's remote identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A restarting router advertises no available bandwidth until it has checked which resources remain. Routers can also send a link identifier only to the neighbor on that link.

sections.title: Security and Assigned Field Numbers
sections.content:
These extensions use OSPFv2 opaque LSAs, which are not used for shortest-path-first computation or normal routing. The RFC says they therefore have no direct effect on IP routing, but tampering with GMPLS traffic-engineering LSAs may affect the underlying optical or SONET-SDH transport network. It recommends securing and authenticating the information.

The RFC introduces four Link sub-TLVs and allocates a top-level type for the Link Local TLV. It notes that the suggested sub-TLV numbers should be granted because interoperable implementations already use them.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing these advertisements does not directly change ordinary IP routing, but it can affect the transport network. The RFC says routers should secure and authenticate the advertised information.
